newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-DIAGANA SOUGHT ENJOYMENT, NOT GOLD.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-DIAGANA SOUGHT ENJOYMENT, NOT GOLD.

text.p: Stephane Diagana came to the world championships just to enjoy himself and ended up with a gold medal.
"My goal was to have some fun running and to make sure I would have no regrets," said Frenchman Diagana on Tuesday, one day after emerging as the surprise winner of the 400 metres hurdles.
"I had really no idea what I was capable of," said the 29-year-old, whose career, featuring many honours but no major title until Monday's win, has been plagued with injury.
"I'm amazed," added Diagana, often a nearly-man with fourth places in the 1992 Olympic final and the 1993 world championships followed by a bronze in the worlds two years ago.

The European record holder, one of the most popular sportsmen in France for his friendly, unassuming nature, missed last year's Olympics after sustaining a stress fracture in his foot which effectively ended his season.
A knee injury this year in his build-up to the world championships then seemed to ruin his hopes of a medal in Athens.
"I was disappointed with my form in the heats but in the semifinals, it was a bit better," he said. "I hoped the final would be okay. It was more than okay.

"I didn't expect to be as successful here but I was looking forward to a good season," he added. "With (American Derrick) Adkins not as good as he used to be and (Zambian Samuel) Matete recovering from injury, I knew there was an opening."

Diagana said one of the factors which helped him win was that he was not under pressure. "I was not the favourite, (American Bryan) Bronson was. I decided to start as fast as I could, then resist. After 200 metres, I started realising it could work."
The Frenchman said having won a title at last should help him reach new heights.
"This is a new start for me," he said. "The motivation was always there but now I know I can do it. That will do my confidence a lot of good."
Diagana, who succeeded German Harald Schmid as the European record holder with 47.37 seconds in 1995, said he would now try to improve that mark.
"I think I can run 47.10," he said.
Asked if he had designs on American Kevin Young's world record of 46.78 set at the 1992 Olympics, he smiled: "Maybe, but perhaps not just yet."
